utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Call the matter, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-42-T, the Prosecutor versus Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any special matter that should be raised at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, during the break we were informed on several occasions by our client of his health problems which he has had over the past 20 days or so. The doctors provided by the Detention Unit examined him. He had blood tests and urine tests several times. He is now receiving medication which is quite strong. As we heard from him -- could we please go into closed session or private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we will go into closed session, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now in open session. My recollection is that there had been a conclusion of your examination of the witness that is presently before the Chamber. Is that so, Mr. Kaufman?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So if we could have the witness then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Welcome back. If I could remind you that you are under affirmation to tell the truth in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we will commence your cross-examination. It's to be Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Allcock. I hope you can hear me.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am attorney Vladimir Petrovic, and I will put a few questions to you on behalf of the accused Strugar in relation to your expert report and your oral testimony before this Tribunal at the end of last year. First of all, I would like to ask you to tell us again what your formal education is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been trained as a sociologist. I graduated in sociology from the University of Leicester and went on to do a master's degree in sociology at Carlton University in Canada and then returned to Britain where I began to teach sociology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope you won't mind my asking you the following question. I have to ask it in view of the contents and range of your report. Your report also deals to a large extent with matters of geography, history, and architecture. These are specific areas which, in my opinion, are not closely connected to your profession. Could you please explain to us how and in what way you feel that you can testify Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. equally competently about matters of history or geography or tourism as competently as you can about matters of sociology?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to answer briefly. My response would run along two lines. The first of these is the brief that I was given by prosecuting counsel in that I understand my -- the function of my report is to provide a broad background information relating to the Old Town of Dubrovnik and its -- its localities, environment and its economic circumstances. In that respect, the skills that I was required to deploy involved really summarising a great deal of uncontentious material. In the past, I've done a training course at Bradford on the work of expert witnesses, and one of the things which was instilled in us is that our function is to assist the Court, and I simply saw my function on this occasion as assisting the Court by assembling uncontentious material which would provide anybody who is not familiar with the Dubrovnik area with the opportunity to familiarise themselves with the main aspects of the situation. In that respect, I suppose, what was more relevant to my role as an expert on that -- within this specific context was not so much my work as a sociologist but the fact that I had been working over a period of ten years in the area of Dubrovnik and, therefore, my direct familiarity with the region was appropriate. The second line along which my response would go is as follows: That this is a problem that I've encountered before, particularly talking with lawyers, and I think there is a tendency to project onto the social science -- scientists certain assumptions about the nature of the social sciences as disciplines which are drawn in fact from the expense of law. I believe there's a much greater degree of specialisation in law than there is in the social sciences. I have neighbours and friends who are lawyers dealing with either the conveyancing of property, commercial law, or family law, and none of them would be seen dead in court defending the work in another specialism, and all of them would be terrified to take your place. This degree of extreme specialisation is not the case in the social sciences, particularly in relation to two disciplines. All social phenomena are located in time and space, and therefore, if one is embarking on a career in any area of social science it's important that one retains an openness towards two disciplines in particular which specialise in time and space; namely, history and geography. As an illustration of this, I think it's probably the case that I can't remember when I last published anything of any significance which did not contain maps. Also, what's particularly important for me is the dimension of time, of history. I do not believe it is possible to understand any social phenomenon without giving a great deal of attention to its historical background, and in this respect my view is not idiosyncratic in any sense but I stand in what I would regard as the core tradition of sociology in which sociology as a discipline has grown up in very close association with history figures such as Max Faber, Emile Dukan [phoen], the person who was my own mentor as an undergraduate, Norbert Elesse [phoen], the person who was my mentor as a master's student in Canada, John Porter. All took very strongly this view that it is essential in attempting to understand anything in society to view that phenomenon, that problem within its historical context. And therefore, I don't believe that in attempting to provide the background, the kind of background information with which I've been dealing in my report on Dubrovnik, that I've been committing any kind of crime of extreme pretension in straying at least marginally into the territory of the historian and the geographer. You particularly also in your question mention the business of architecture. My response in that respect would be slightly different in that I believe that no civilised human being can count themselves as such if they do not have some awareness of their built environment. I claim no special expertise in this area, and indeed what I have done in commenting very briefly on architecture in my report is simply, once again, to summarise what I understand to be a taken-for-granted consensus about those factors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Allcock. Keeping in mind our time constraints, please reply as concisely as possible to my questions. I do appreciate your reply, but I would like to ask you to continue answering very concisely. Am I right in saying, then, when you say that you are more expert in the field of sociology than you are in the field of architecture? Would that be a correct conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this also -- does this also have to do with geography and history?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I return to the point that I've already made, that what I have been trying to do in my report is not to advance the borders of historical and geographical knowledge but simply to provide the taken-for-granted consensus among scholars about the nature of the region which is the subject of my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Am I correct in saying that your viewpoints on non-sociological areas are standpoints that have been taken over from the fund of knowledge that a person of broad general culture would know, or do you have any specific knowledge that would make you more qualified in this area than in other areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there are two things in that respect I would reply. First of all, if I have more than an average layability in these areas, it rests upon my familiarity with the area and the fact that I lived and worked intermittently in and around Dubrovnik over some substantial period of time and therefore what I have to say is based on judgements with the -- based on familiarity with the area and not simply on things that I've picked up in books. The second point I would make in replying is not intended to be aggressive but perhaps might come across a little bit more so, and that is that because I believe that what I have offered here is -- is an uncontentious consensus, I think it's open to -- to counsel to produce some kind of evidence that what I have offered is less than acceptable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will give you some matters later on. Now I'm only focusing on the general background. For example, I'm interested in the historical context of the early Middle Ages, the Middle Ages, the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Is this a result of your study of these historical periods or just the result of a more or less detailed summary of something in a historical textbook or tourist guide or similar publication?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assure counsel that I was not present in Dubrovnik during the Middle Ages, but as it should be evident from my report, I've given footnotes on several occasions to the scholarly works on which I've relied in putting together this report. I remind counsel that in that respect I've relied heavily on the work of the late Frank Carter, whose study of Dubrovnik is probably unrivaled by anything else produced in Britain, the various works of John Fine, who is an American historian of very high reputation, and the work of Yugoslav historians as well, such as Barisa Krekic and others. So that I -- in setting out to write this report, I didn't sit down and rely on tourist guides, I took the trouble to acquaint myself with substantial works of scholarship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This study of history, is it something that you have engaged in before or is this something that you have done now for the first time for the purposes of this expert report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already indicated in my response to your earlier question, I have seen it as appropriate in my work as a sociologist always to involve myself in the study of the historical background of whatever it is I'm working on. My first scholarly acquaintance with Yugoslavia began in, I think, 1967, and in the variety of projects which I've pursued since then, I've invariably attempted to place the work that I've been doing within its Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. historical context, and I continued this when I began in 1981 to work on the questions of tourism. And so that the -- my venture into history on this occasion, which counsel is attempting to suggest, I think, is somehow capricious on my part, is an indication of a consistent stance which I have taken from my position as a scholar in the area, and this is by no means -- this is the first occasion on which I've indeed looked at the history of Dubrovnik. I published much earlier than this a paper on the history of tourism, which is included in my CV, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may ask you, have you published any works in, for example, the field of architecture or the field of geography, or exclusively in the field of history or is everything that you have done in the context of your study of tourism and other sociological research?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I'll remind you of the answer that I've already given about the relatively open boundaries of sociology. One of the first scholarly works that I published was at the invitation of Professor Frank Carter, which was a contribution to a work which has become a major standard in its field, The Historical Geography of the Balkans. Professor Carter was a geographer and yet invited me as a sociologist, because of my familiarity with the material with which I was dealing, to contribute in that area. And there have been a number of other occasions on which, similarly, the work that I have done has extended across disciplinary boundaries, not only history, geography, but also political science. Some of the more recent work which I've done since the unfortunate process of the disintegration of Yugoslavia began was conducted in association and collaboration with political scientists. And perhaps one minor point of detail would be relevant here, in that in 1973 I moved into the humanities department in Bradford which was expressly a department of interdisciplinary human studies. The tradition of that department was to emphasise to students and to foster among staff an awareness of the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration. The questions that counsel is asking indicate a certain surprise that these things might be possible, but I assure him that these things are relatively normal within the academic field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to assure you that I am familiar with this, but I would also like to say that I can conclude only one thing from what you have said: Your profession -- your professional field is sociology and everything else is auxiliary to that, something that helps you in conducting your research in your professional field. Every job is multi-disciplinary. What we are doing here is multi-disciplinary, but although I will put questions to you in the field of history, I will not for a second call myself an expert on history or on geography, and that is the crux of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am loath to interject because I understand that the Court is not minded to hear too many objections in this matter, but I feel that counsel for the Defence gave a speech rather than request a question there. Perhaps counsel for the Defence would like to phrase a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think there is substance in what you say, Mr. Kaufman, but I don't think there is reason for us to be too technical at this preliminary stage of the questioning. There is, as I understand it, a general exploration by Mr. Petrovic of the qualifications and experience of the witness in this general field, and while a lengthy speech-like question is not terribly helpful for us, it is one way of helping Mr. Petrovic get the points that he wishes to make across on this general topic before he moves on, as I'm sure he will shortly, to -- to more direct issues that he wishes to raise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please just give me an answer, then.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm slightly puzzled as to what the question was, but I think the most appropriate response that I can make is to say well, the best test of my knowledge of the area and the capacity to -- my capacity to write the report that I have given is in specific areas rather than at the level of extreme generality that was discussed in the speech at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Allcock, could you tell me -- I mean, if I followed this very carefully, what are the exact materials that the Prosecutor gave you while you were preparing this expert opinion that we've been discussing, if any, that is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall being given any materials by the Prosecutor. I had a letter in which the purpose of the report was outlined. That was subsequently reduced somewhat in its scope because, as counsel will know, the range of issues covered in the indictment were reduced at one point in the period leading up to this case, and you will recall that at the beginning of my first appearance in front of the Court a number of photographs were also -- and maps were also put before the Court, and the evening before I appeared in the Court, Mr. Kaufman asked me if I would mind if he used my presence as an opportunity to introduce those materials to the Court as evidence, and I replied I had no objection whatsoever to that. But apart from that, the -- I don't believe that the Prosecutor's office have given me any instructions as to -- they certainly offered me no material which ought to appear or that I ought to use in the preparation of my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now I'd like to move on to something else and then perhaps later during the course of the day we will be able to go back to some of the things that we've been discussing just now. I would like to move on to some concrete questions related to your paper. First of all, I would like to ask you: What Yugoslav scholars did you cite, or, rather, scholars from the territory of the former Yugoslavia, to be precise, in your expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the preparation of this report, I recall using -- well, I've already mentioned the work of Barisa Krekic. There is a work by somebody called Peric on the history of Dubrovnik, specifically on that topic. I used that. I used a number of public reference materials, atlases, statistical yearbooks, and so on. I was sent, at my request, from the library of the faculty for tourism and foreign trade in Dubrovnik a couple of articles which are also cited in the footnotes of my paper, in particular one by the head of the faculty, Professor Kovacic. What else? Oh, yes, in relation to the political area, I've also had the opportunity to look in particular at some work by Professor Kasapovic from University of Zagreb, and also a couple of historians, Mr. Goldstein's History of Croatia. I think those -- those are the only ones that come to mind immediately, but the works that I've used in general are listed in the footnotes of my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So could you please give me brief answers, because I'm not expecting any long answers. Could you briefly tell me when the Dubrovnik Republic was established, on that basis, and give me some general elements related to the history of the Dubrovnik Republic as an independent entity. Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want something very brief, then this is outlined in my report. The republic really emerges as such in the thirteenth century. Its existence is based upon trade, and its political organisation was based on the status and wealth, indeed, of a few powerful families within the republic. It persisted as an independent republic under the patronage and toleration of surrounding powers, particularly Venice and the Ottoman Empire, up until the beginning of the nineteenth century when the republic was finally extinguished by the activities of Napoleon. I hope that is sufficiently brief for you, but if not, we can --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That will do, thank you. In your report on page 5 there is something I found to be of interest. So could you please have a look at the report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Could I compare the B/C/S version to the English version for a moment, please. So in the English version it is page 3, actually. Paragraph 1. Paragraph 1 on page 3 of the English version. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is the paragraph that starts with the Empire of Stefan Dusan Nemanjic, and then you refer to the complexity and relations between Dubrovnik and the Venetian overlords and the Slav states and its hinterland. So could you tell me briefly what their relations were like?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're -- I'm aware of your requirement for a brief answer. I think the way -- the best way in which to frame this briefly is that the dominant power in the Adriatic Sea was the Venetian republic. The dominant power from the end of the fourteenth century in the Balkan hinterland was the Ottoman Empire, and the republic of Dubrovnik found itself at the awkward conjunction of these two important forces. Also, of course, the Austro-Hungarian Empire had a significant presence in the region so that the -- the political future of the republic of Dubrovnik throughout that entire period of its existence as an independent republic depended upon either the skill of its leaders or their good fortune in steering some kind of acceptable course between these three powerful influences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm perplexed now. It is not clear to me on the basis of your answer what the time frame is, so my question is: When did the Austro-Hungarian Empire come into being? Or, rather, I'm sorry, when did the Austrian Empire become the Austro-Hungarian Empire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check the date of that. I can't give you a spontaneous answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me the century?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're talking about the Empire -- see, this is actually a more complex question than counsel indicates --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a second, please. I'm putting a very formal question to you. There is an exact year when the Austrian Empire became the Austro-Hungarian Empire. When did this happen, and in which century did this happen? It's quite simple, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of a complex transition between the ownership of an extensive array of feudal lands by the Habsburgs and evolution into an Empire. I wouldn't be able to give you a precise date at which one would say -- it could be declared to be the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there not a generally accepted date for that historical transition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may well be, Your Honour, but I'm not aware of it at the moment. I would need to check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the century when this occurred? So in which century did the Austrian Empire formally become the Austro-Hungarian Empire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think this is probably the sixteenth century.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will have to disappoint you and tell you that it happened three centuries later. So now in that context - this actually happened in 1867. This is the year when the Austrian Empire became the Austro-Hungarian Empire. That is to say, when this Empire came into being consisting of Austria and Hungary. So now I'm asking you about the relations between Austro-Hungary and the independent republic of Dubrovnik. Could you tell me how is this possible, if we know that Austro-Hungary came into being in the second half of the nineteenth century, by then the independent republic of Dubrovnik was no longer in existence. It was actually part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire for a long time by then.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the nature of the confusion here arises from my allusion of two facts. One is of course that the -- I have used the phrase the Austro-Hungarian Empire to cover the development of Habsburg possessions in the area. I'm sure counsel is correct in citing 1867 as the date at which this -- this entity actually adopted the title Austro-Hungarian Empire, but the Habsburg dynasty in that area are of much greater antiquity than this, going back into the Middle Ages, and I apologise if the looseness of my phraseology has elided that transition. Your puzzlement about the role of Austria in the area is cleared up when I point out that what I had in mind was the role of the house of Habsburg and its various possessions and not the entity which you have correctly pointed out didn't take that title until later on. But I should say incidentally that the -- much more important than Habsburg possessions in the evolution of the Republic of Ragusa was the point that I've already made about the need to -- the position of Ragusa --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Please, there is no need to elaborate in such detail. Could you please just give specific answers to my questions. You have already said what you wished to say, and my colleagues are going to put questions to you if they deem it necessary. So could you please answer my questions if the Trial Chamber allows them to be put the way I'm putting them. So let us deal with the nineteenth century briefly. The beginning of the nineteenth century, the first half of the nineteenth century, the second half of the nineteenth century. What are the neighbouring states of the Dubrovnik Republic and what is their status?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the first half of the nineteenth century Venice was still the dominant power in the northern part of the Adriatic. The Ottoman Empire controlled the area which is now Bosnia and a substantial part of the Balkan Peninsula inland. Actually, Croatia which lay to the north of Dubrovnik in the late -- was attached to the Hungarian crown, and although a number of people have often said, well, what about Montenegro, Montenegro didn't have at that time any kind of adjacent border with Dubrovnik, and indeed was an extremely small entity indeed so I shall discount Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Allcock, I'm sorry, but I have to interrupt you yet again. And, again, I need to point out some major shortcomings in your report. I asked you about the first half of the nineteenth century. The first fact that is wrong is that in the first half of the nineteenth century, the republic of Venice was no longer in existence. It had been abolished by Napoleon considerably before that in the eighteenth century?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was concentrating on your earlier question at that point. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, the second mistake you made was the fact that you spoke about Croatia as part of the Hungarian crown. That is also not correct. This took place only in 1868, after the agreement reached between Croatia and Hungary. So that is considerably later.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a matter of considerable historical dispute. The -- the crown of Croatia passed to Hungary in the twelfth century. I'm puzzled. Certainly there was a change of its status in 1868 but the relationship between Croatia and Hungary is of considerably greater antiquity than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of document was made in 1868 between Croatia and Hungary? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there's disagreement about the status of that among historians. The eminent historian C. A. MacCartney said that the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you yet again. That document, what is the name of that document --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and what is included in this document? What are its contents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read the document, I've only read secondary accounts of it, but I understand that it does spell out the relationship, among other things, between the Croatian lands and the Hungarian crown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these regulations regulated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- Croatia continued to have its own -- its own assembly, its own Sabor. Croatia continued to be governed by a governor, a ban, and there were -- it was possible for representatives of the Croatian nobility in particular to be represented within the Hungarian parliament, within the Hungarian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the state and legal relationship between Croatia and Hungary or, rather, between Croatia and Austro-Hungary later?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the matter of the most extreme --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise for interjecting. Once again questions have been asked on the expertise of this witness in matters of geography and history. I would, however, strongly object to questions being asked on legal matters since later this week Your Honours will hear from a witness who will testify as to the legal status of Croatia at certain times relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Kaufman. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I'm not asking the witness to give a legal opinion or legal assessment. I'm asking a man who claims to be familiar with the history of a region to give me relevant historic facts. I'm not asking for any legal qualifications or any other such thing. I'm simply interested in the historical relationship between Croatia and Hungary. So please do allow this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I propose to allow the questions to continue, Mr. Kaufman, for much the same reason as I indicated a little time ago. I'm understanding these questions to be put in an historical context rather than a legal, but the point is being reached, can I indicate, Mr. Petrovic, where I might ask you what is the relevance of all this. I won't ask it yet, because you go on for a little while, but nothing --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- nothing has yet been said that would indicate to me what might be the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, even before you put the question, I will take the liberty of explaining why I'm putting this question. By your leave, of course. I am putting these questions for a simple reason. Notwithstanding the deep respect I have for this witness, I am trying to show, and I believe that I have succeeded in doing so considerably so far, that the gentleman who is an expert witness in this case simply does not have the knowledge that is required of an expert witness in this area. Believe me, anybody who completed elementary school or secondary school in the countries of the former Yugoslavia knows the answers to these questions. I must say, regrettably, that your expert witness who is a knowledgeable man in the field of tourism is not a proper expert in the subject matter involved here. I do not wish to offend anyone, but that is the core of the matter. Believe me, I am no expert in history either, but the questions I am putting have to do with things I learned in secondary school. So by your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you may continue for a little time. I would suggest that if you are wanting to put matters of historical fact as you understand them to the witness, matters which you believe the witness has wrongly understood or which are relevant to his report or which you suggest would demonstrate that he has not an adequate familiarity with the history of the region, that you might put those matters shortly and simply and then move on to matters that are more relevant directly to the circumstances of this case. Is that clear enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course, of course I shall do that. However, I am bound by the report that I have here in front of me. Four or five pages in the B/C/S version deal with the historical context. I share your view that this is not of key importance for this case, but this is part of the report that was submitted by the other side, and it was admitted, so I have to deal with it. And of course I fully share your views that your ruling with regard to this particular legal matter will not hinge on what this report contains, but I will just put a few more questions in this regard and then I'm going to move on to another area which may be of greater interest, another area contained in this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Allcock, we were talking about the state and legal relationship between Hungary and Croatia. Can you tell us what this relationship was like?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a problem here in satisfying your demand for brevity and the demand for completeness. The entire domestic political history of Croatia in the nineteenth century, to my mind, seems to have revolved around the difference of interpretation of exactly what was contained within that -- within that document. Croatian nationalists have always maintained that the Nagodba set them up as acknowledging their independence as a state and acknowledging the continuous existence of a Croatian state from much earlier times, and Hungarian experts, on the other hand, always maintained that Croatia had been simply, in one form or another, assimilated into the Hungarian state, and there were long and bitter disagreements between both sides which do in some respect continue to shape Croatian politics today about precisely that issue. And I do think that I cannot satisfy your request for brevity in answering that question any more completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We were talking about the troubled relationship with the hinterland and with other neighbours. Let us deal with the hinterland now. Can you tell me about the hinterland? What countries existed there, and to be more precise, I'm interested in the eighteenth, nineteenth, and twentieth centuries specifically, the continental hinterland of Dubrovnik. Could you tell me what states existed there and how they came into being and how they eventually disappeared?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Ottoman Empire was established from the middle to the late fourteenth century in the Balkans. I'm not certain exactly at what date it acquired a common frontier with the Republic of Ragusa. Then during the nineteenth century, of course, the status of Bosnia as part or as a component of the Ottoman Empire came into question. There was an important rebellion in 1874 which continued for a couple of years which resulted in the end, in the granting of Bosnia and Herzegovina to Austro-Hungary under the status of protectorate. This was subsequent in 1908 turned into a direct annexation. Montenegro, further south, began as a -- having virtually no international legal recognition, although it did sustain a -- a relatively independent, a relatively independent existence for a long time, first of all as an independent ecclesiastical institution under prince bishops. I am -- I think I'm right in saying that the first international recognition of Montenegro as a state did not occur until 1878. Is that a sufficiently complete answer to the question or do you want to go on into the twentieth century?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I'd just like to ask you about the year. In which year was Bosnia-Herzegovina occupied?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina occupied under the terms of the -- the Congress of Berlin, 1878.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to move on to somebody else. Just a moment, please. I would just like to deal with history very briefly a bit more, if it's all right with you. Tell me, please, when the Austro-Hungarian monarchy disintegrated, what happened to Dubrovnik in those years after that, before the First World War and after the Second World War. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crucial change took place in the First World War when the previous different states, Croatia, Bosnia, Montenegro, were brought into a common south Slav state, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, at the end of 1919. Dubrovnik at that stage, of course, had already been incorporated into Croatia prior to that. Its independent existence had ceased as counsel has already correctly pointed out and as indeed I acknowledge in my report with the activities of Napoleon. It was not a separate state then and simply was taken into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes along with the unification of the other south Slav lands in 1918.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard about the state of the Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs? Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The unification process was a complex process, and indeed in the later months of the First World War it became evident that it was going to have to be necessary to find some kind of alternative to the previous Austro-Hungarian dominion in the Balkans, and to cut a long story short, two focuses appeared initially. The -- there was the -- in early -- earlier in 1918, there was an attempt based on -- around the activities of Slovene representatives in the Reichstag to organise some kind of state, but this was then subordinated later on because the -- that was intended to involve simply the south Slav peoples which had previously been part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and that is a different entity from the entity which was subsequently created by bringing in the Serbian and Montenegrin states and -- which produced the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes by which the state was eventually known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the Austro-Hungarian monarchy fall apart?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again we're talking about -- about process here. I'm not quite sure what date you've give to the actual termination of it, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. That is also part of general knowledge, when the Austro-Hungarian Empire dissolved. Everybody knows that. When? What year? At what time? What events led to this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we being technical here? It certainly would have been 1918, but I can't give a precise date to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your previous response to my previous question you say earlier in 1918 there was an attempt based around the activities of Slovene representatives. Is that when the break-up of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the -- in effect the disintegration of the Austro-Hungarian Empire happened before then, but when its actual legal termination was, again I'm talking legally here, I don't know. There was a period of a few months between the creation of the state to which you've referred and the eventual unification of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As someone with pretensions to deal with historical issues, do you know the day of -- the date of the armistice in World War I?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the eleventh of the eleventh, isn't it, 1918. 11th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must tell you that that is not so. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the date it's celebrated in Britain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion -- I withdraw this. Tell me, please, what was the sequence of internationally recognised state entities, I'm talking about the Austro-Hungarian monarchy and ending with Yugoslavia, so I'm interested particularly in Dubrovnik. These are very precise matters. We don't need to go into any wider explanations here.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't understood your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will try to clarify it. What government authorities changed in Dubrovnik between 1914 and 1920? Who ruled Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had thought this was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the formal legal state sense. I'm talking about internationally recognised states and their sequence in that area. So what happened after the break-up of the Austro-Hungarian Empire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had thought that this sort of information was relevant to my report, I would have investigated it in greater detail. I didn't think that those events had very much bearing on the situation in question and, therefore, I did not take the trouble to investigate that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Allcock, a third of your report is history, the history of Dubrovnik. You even mention this. Look at page 5 of your report, paragraph 1. You speak of the disintegration of the Empire, the end of World War I and the states that arose. Look on page 5 of the English version, paragraph 1. So you deal with this. I don't see how you can then be surprised by my questions, because you dealt with this in your report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only surprise is in the nature of detail which counsel considers to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to enter into an argument with you, but I think these are elementary questions. However, I will not go any further with this line of questioning. You mentioned the French General Marmont in one place -- and this is my last question to do with history. Rather, I have two more historical questions. I hope you don't mind. Could you please tell me, very briefly, in Dubrovnik, Marmont, 1806, could you just give us a brief sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation again is complex. A lot -- there is a lot of confusion among historians, and I understand the nature of your question here because there is a great deal of confusion among historians about the precise date which the Republic of Dubrovnik ceased to exist. A number of historians cite 1805 as that date and the confusion -- I investigated this in particular because contradictory dates are given. Often -- I believe historians take the -- the Treaty of Presburg in December 1805 when Venice was -- the power of Venice in the area was extinguished, as indicating that Dubrovnik also ceased to exist as a state in 1805. This is not actually correct. The French troops didn't actually enter Dubrovnik until May - I think it was the 27th of May - 1806. And even at that point Napoleon declared that this did not affect the independence of the Republic of Dubrovnik, and he did not actually declare that Dubrovnik had ceased to exist until 1808, however I think it's fairly clear that the 27th of May, 1806, when French troops actually occupied the town, is a pretty convincing date of which we can say that the independence of the Republic of Ragusa ceased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will put forward a conclusion and then I will say that your knowledge of history is extremely fragmentary. You know details such as the 27th of May, 1806, and yet you are not aware of the sequence of governments or states on the territory of Dubrovnik. Tell me, with regard to the Russian fleet at that time, briefly, if you can in one sentence, if not, then I will withdraw my question: Where did the Russian fleet appear and when?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the Russian fleet was active in the area at that time because they were supporting the Montenegrins, but exactly where they were at that time, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Russian fleet sailed into the Boka Kotorska bay and the clashes between Boka and the Dubrovnik territory, do you know something about this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand there was some fighting of that kind. I didn't think it was sufficiently relevant to the general flow of events for me to investigate it further and to write it up in my report. One has to make some sort of decisions about relevance and my understanding, as I said at the beginning of this questioning, was to provide some sense of the general shape of the history of the area, and in that sense perhaps I have conveyed the impression of fragmentariness, but -- okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must ask you why you agreed to provide general information about something that you obviously have not mastered, because I am sure that you're an eminent expert in your own field, but why did you agree to write about something that is evidently not your field?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer to this is possibly more simple than you think it is. A general introductory report of the kind that I've prepared touches on a number of issues, not only history but also economics and politics as well as specific issues relating to tourism. It would have been considerably more time-consuming for this Court, and indeed expensive, had the Prosecution commissioned four different witnesses to put together the background material that they did. They made a judgement, based on earlier contact on my part with the Prosecutor's office, that I could provide the range of information which they needed with the succinctness that they required, and I -- bearing in mind the fact that I was not appearing as a professional historian but as a social scientist with a broad familiarity with the area, its economics, historical and political background, under those terms, I agreed. If I had been engaged specifically as a historian or invited to be engaged as a historian specifically in order to provide an extremely detailed defensible account of the history of the area, I would have declined that invitation. I received, however, a different invitation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the reason you deal with history here is the fact that there was an effort to save money on the preparation of the report. Is that your standpoint?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you better ask the Prosecutor's office about that. I simply received an invitation to which I responded in the terms in which it was presented to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting this to you because you yourself said that it was more economical and simple for all this to be done by you rather than engaging a historian, a geographer, and so on. So those are your words. You say that you were invited because it was cheaper than having a historian as well. Maybe I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my surmise, not a point which was put to me by the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. My last historical question: The organisation of the newly formed Yugoslav state, how was it organised in 1918?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1918. Well, there was a long period in which its organisation was under discussion. The constitutional commission didn't -- constitutional assembly didn't deliver its conclusions until, I think, 1920, 1921. So there was a long period then in which Yugoslavia was under some kind of provisional arrangement. In effect, the -- as I understand it, various people who took responsibility for ministries, if this is what you're getting at, was provided by a more or less informal selection among the various interest groups who had been present in the formulation of Yugoslavia, from the Yugoslav committee, the government of Serbia, former members of the various state assemblies from the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and so on. It wasn't -- it didn't acquire a proper constitutional standing until the Vidovdan constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the territorial organisation of the first Yugoslav state?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a unified state. It didn't have at that stage either the federal structure which it acquired in the post Second World War period or even the organisation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- have you heard of the term "banovina"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is the organisation which was imposed by King Aleksandar after he took control of the country under the dictatorship. He divided the country into a number regions which expressly cut across historical linguistic boundaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know what unit Dubrovnik was a part of at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's Primorska, but I might be wrong about that. I think it's Primorska. No, it was Zetska. I knew I'd get that wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the banovina of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the attempt to modify that structure which was introduced, I believe, in 1938 when, after a prolonged period in which various Croatian parties had expressed their dissatisfaction with the situation in Croatia within Yugoslavia, an agreement was reached between the Prime Minister Cvetkovic and the head of the Croatian peasant party Vlado Macek, and it was agreed that some of the former territories, not only historical Croatia, but also parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, should be joined together into a single governorship, banovina Hrvatska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that was part of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you're wrong again. It was.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now I will move on. My second topic will be shorter, but perhaps the Chamber feels this is a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic, it is. I see that from your client, and we will have periods of a little less than an hour and a half for the balance of the day. You will, of course, remember that you need to finish in time for re-examination to conclude the evidence today. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Allcock, if you don't mind, I would now like to deal with some geographical aspects of your report which I believe are simpler than the ones we dealt with before the break. Would you please tell me the length of the territory of the municipality of Dubrovnik. How long is it, approximately, from the far south to the far north-west points?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred in my report to an approximate figure of 120 kilometres. This is an approximate figure. And I think since you've raised the question, it would be useful to point out that this is an informal estimate as the crow flies for directly and not the length of the coastline, which is much longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about the depth of the territory of Dubrovnik municipality, the 20 kilometres or so, how does it vary and how deep is the territory at various points?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it varies extremely. I gather at one point it's down to about 50 metres, but the figure you've already mentioned, I thought it was a little less than that at its widest point, a little less than 20 kilometres and more like 15, but that's the general order of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise. Either I made a mistake in my question or it was misinterpreted. I don't remember having mentioned 20 kilometres, but -- there was a misunderstanding. I was referring to the total length of 120 kilometres. So what is the narrowest point of this territory and the broadest point of this territory? Maybe it's clearer now.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't alter the answer I gave before which is that I believe the extreme southern limit down near Prevlaka gets down to about 50 metres, but the -- I think the widest point is about 15 kilometres. Again, this has been an informal measure across the map on my part rather than a scientific measurement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We will agree, then, that there are quite a few places then where the width of the territory is a kilometre -- up to a kilometre, a few hundred metres, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, in the hinterland behind the narrowest parts of the territory, what other geographical entities are there; Montenegro, Bosnia? Do you know something about this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at its most southern point, the territory of the municipality abuts onto the Republic of Montenegro, but for the greater part of the hinterland there is a common border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and in particular the area known as Herzegovina. Is this sufficiently precise for your needs?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you. Can you tell me what there is at the extreme south of the Dubrovnik municipality? What geographical phenomenon exists on the far south of Dubrovnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose the -- the only geographical feature of any major significance I figure was the Bay of Kotor. Is this not what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I had in mind. But to be more precise, what is there -- what part of the territory is at the very entrance to the Boka Kotorska bay, which is at the same time is the southernmost point of Dubrovnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume you're referring to the Prevlaka peninsula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you describe very briefly the geographical characteristics of that part of the territory of Dubrovnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Prevlaka peninsula?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never actually visited it, but I understand from illustrations I've seen, descriptions of it, it's a very low-lying and thin promontory that projects across the entrance to the Bay of Kotor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the borderline between the municipality of Dubrovnik and the neighbouring municipality in Montenegro? How does it run?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer -- I can't answer that with specific detail, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The southernmost part of Dubrovnik municipality, with what municipality in Montenegro does it border?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't answer that. I know what the -- I know what the settlements around the bay, there are places like Resan and so on, but I don't know which municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the nearest town is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably Herceg Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the municipality is also called Herceg Novi.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the southernmost point, do you know what the border is between Herceg Novi municipality and Dubrovnik municipality? So I'm discussing the municipalities of Dubrovnik and Herceg Novi. Does the border run along the edge or does it run across the sea? Do you know how the border runs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it runs roughly at right angles to the sea, but again, I haven't looked at this with any care.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This means, if I understand you correctly, that as far as you know, the territory of Dubrovnik municipality does not protrude into the Boka Kotorska bay if the border runs at right angles to the sea or, rather, through the coastline.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already indicated the territory of Dubrovnik runs into the Prevlaka peninsula. I'm slightly puzzled about what the nature of the question is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is perhaps slightly complex, but believe me, it's very important.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would help, wouldn't it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it would. But before I show you the map, I just want to ask you about something that you might very well know. I will try to be as simple -- put it as simply as possible. Does even a foot of Dubrovnik municipality protrude into the Boka Kotorska bay or does the border run directly towards the sea? I don't know if I can put it any clearer than that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question, and I can't answer it precisely. I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the key factor among the reasons that pertain to the essence of the conflicts -- conflict in this area is precisely this fact? Does even a foot of the territory of Dubrovnik municipality touch the sea or not? Have you heard of this dispute, this issue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware there has been a protracted international dispute between the Republic of Croatia and subsequently the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia about exactly where the border should run in that area, but it's not an area, it's not a topic which I've felt that I wanted to research in any -- with any care. I've not needed to look into that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about the nature of this dispute?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with care. A colleague of mine, Malcolm Milivojevic, has been working on this and has written something about it, but precisely because he's been attending to it, I have not thought it appropriate to take up this topic for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise. Would you say who this gentleman is and what he has to do with you and your testimony here, or maybe he has no connection and I misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only reason for mentioning his name is that he is a colleague of mine at Bradford. He has a honourary research fellowship and he has done a number of projects concerning military and intelligence affairs. I'm not introducing his paper on the topic as evidence into this Court at all. What I'm simply saying is that because there has to be a division of labour between people in a very small research unit. If somebody is looking at a topic, I don't feel obliged to follow their tracks, but simply let them get on with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what Mr. Milivojevic's contribution was to the report you drafted, if any?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you refer to Mr. Milivojevic in your paper, in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I do, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible I might have cited one of his papers, but I don't remember doing so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest we move on. In your report, you also mention the architectural heritage of Dubrovnik, and I am inclined to conclude that we have the same -- the same problems with this part of your report that we had when you dealt with history, and that is that you reported on something that is not your professional field, but I will not burden you or the Chamber with this. I will move on to what I believe really is your professional field in which I do not doubt that you are an eminent expert, and that is the issue of tourism. And I will try to put a few questions to you which I deem to be important. Would you please tell us something in general explaining the influence and mutual connection between the armed conflict which occurs in an area, any area, and the consequences for tourism in the area. For example, there is conflict on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. What are the repercussions of this, for example, on tourism in northern Greece, if any?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tourism is notoriously sensitive to disturbances of any kind. Tourists will not go to areas not only where there is an armed conflict but where there is risk of disease or even a serious inconvenience. It was notable during the two armed conflicts relating to Iraq over recent years that there's been a dramatic drop in trans-Atlantic tourism associated with both of those events even though the chances of trans-Atlantic passengers being involved in armed conflict are virtually zero. There was an occasion a few years ago, I forget exactly when it was now the mid 1980s when several stories about the hygiene of Yugoslav resorts appeared in the German press and there was a short-term but dramatic drop in the number of German tourists coming to Yugoslavia. Therefore, any disturbance in an area has an adverse consequence for the flow of tourists. And if you look at my report, I've tried to convey this in certainly one of the figures towards the end. I think it's figure 1. Yes, figure 1 on page 17, where you can see there that the decline in the numbers of tourists and the number of nights they spent in Croatia began to decline as early as 1988 but certainly conspicuously so in 1989. Obviously this was before any armed conflict was present in the area but certainly this was already a time at which political instability was evident. And therefore, I think it's important to realise that the presence of armed conflict in Yugoslavia only extends and intensifies this effect which you can see very clearly from that table that by the time we get to 1991, there is indeed a catastrophic drop in the number of tourists who come to the area and the time they spend there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll go back to that subject a bit later, but you just referred to some figures, so could you please explain them to me. Just a moment, please. Let me find it in the English version. Just a moment, please. I would like to indicate exactly where it is. Yes. It is page 12 of your report. Please, would you look at the top of page 12.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand your report correctly, the most dramatic fall in the number of tourists took place in Dubrovnik before the armed conflict broke out. That's right. That's what you say here. Eight hundred ninety-two -- 892.579 visitors in the city in 1987 had declined to 33.489 in 1990. Have I quoted your report properly? That's the end of page 12 -- the end of page 11, rather, and the beginning of page 12. The first sentence on page 12.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And as you can see from -- the course of events in Dubrovnik followed the general shape of the graph that I've given on page 17, although the figures on page 17 refer to the situation in Croatia as a whole and not to Dubrovnik in particular, but you'd see exactly the same shape of the curve, I think, if you looked at figures confined to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand things correctly, the number of tourists declined about 30 times in 1990 in relation to 1987, approximately, from 892.000 to 33.000, approximately. So it is roughly about 30 times less; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a catastrophic decline, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this happened in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the process began earlier than this, as the graph shows, because as I've already mentioned, tourists were aware of the increasing instability of Yugoslavia over the years previous to the outbreak of any actual fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you will agree with me in the following assessment, that the most dramatic decline, that is to say of 3.000 per cent in bed/nights in Dubrovnik occurred before the conflict; from 1987 to 1990. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The response was a general response to the instability in Yugoslavia and to events happening more generally in the former Yugoslavia and not specifically to events happening in Dubrovnik. That is correct if that's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you've given me an answer already, but I want to be quite sure that this is what your answer is. So the most dramatic decline, one of 30 times, happened before a single bullet was fired in Dubrovnik and in the surrounding area. Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, and my understanding is that fighting broke out in October of that year, which would be after the end of the tourist season.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the year? What was the year when this happened? When did the fighting start?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking just about Dubrovnik or about Croatia in general?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that toward the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the interpretation I was listening to into B/C/S went wrong, but anyway. Not only in Dubrovnik but in the entire area of the former Yugoslavia there was no armed conflict practically in the territory of the entire former Yugoslavia in 1990. Well, not practically but completely.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were disturbances. I remember when I drove down the Dalmatian coast in the May of that year, during the period of the referendum on independence of Croatia, there were a whole succession of military and police roadblocks down that area because of disturbances which were happening inland. This was not, you know, formal armed conflict in the sense of a war, but sporadic outbreaks of violence of a more localised nature at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Allcock, I have to correct you. I have to draw your attention to a mistake that you keep making. I believe it's unintentional. I don't wish to believe that you are doing this on purpose. In which year did the referendum take place in Croatia? According to what you said in your previous answer, it seems that the referendum took place in 1990. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. If I've conveyed that impression, that is an inadvertent slip of the tongue. 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. That's right, yes. But in response to my question, you were saying that your impression of 1990 actually referred to 1991. So I'm going back to the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry about that. 1991 is the -- I'm not sure where 1990 came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1990, nothing happened. Perhaps there are certain political processes that are taking place but not processes that would mean an armed conflict of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But as I've indicated in my answer to earlier questions, tourism is extremely sensitive with respect to the anticipation of disturbances of all kinds. So the speculation that was taking place -- I mean, in Britain this began, I suppose, in about 1989, following the fall of the Berlin Wall as to what the future of Yugoslavia would now be, and I think that the response of tourists to that kind of instability, you know, is not something which you just see in Britain. It's something that extends across Europe and the United States.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go back to the period that followed the period of conflicts in the area of Dubrovnik, as we call it. I would like to emphasise that I am not asking you about what happened in the area of the municipality of Dubrovnik, because you were not there. I'm asking you about tourism and Dubrovnik after the conflict in Dubrovnik. So please do not deal with what happened in Dubrovnik. Just give me the following answer: In 1993 and in 1994, the armed conflict was in full sway [sic] in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's only a couple of hundred metres away from Dubrovnik in some parts, and then there are conflicts in eastern Slavonia, western Slavonia, in Krajina, but in the area surrounding Dubrovnik, there are no conflicts. So the conflicts that took place 500 metres or a kilometre away from Dubrovnik, did that crucially affect the tourism situation in Dubrovnik? We're not talking about Dubrovnik itself now, but the fact that there is a war is taking place 500 metres away from Dubrovnik, does this crucially affect the arrival or non-arrival of tourists in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, the continuing difficulties, armed conflicts throughout the whole of the region for several years afterwards will have slowed the rate of recovery of tourism. I refer you once again to the graph I've given on page 17, and you can see from the figures that are given there for the years 1992, 3, 4, there's a very slow return of tourists to the Dalmatian coast, even after Croatia is no longer directly involved in the war, and indeed I ceased to do direct research on this area at around this time, but my understanding is that certainly in a number of areas of the Dalmatian coast, if not the entire area, we've barely got back to those 1987, 1988 years in terms of the volume of international tourism. It takes a very long time to recover in an area which is so internationally competitive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you will agree with me when I say that had there not been a conflict at all in the Dalmatian coast, the vicinity of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have affected tourism in such a way in the Dalmatian region that it would -- the number of tourists would have been dramatically smaller in this entire period that we're discussing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is so, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you -- just a moment, please. I'm sorry. It was my understanding that you are very familiar with Dubrovnik, that you spent a considerable part of your life there so that I can put some questions to you that pertain to the town itself and that you refer to in your report. Believe me, I think you will find this easier, and I think it will be easier to deal with these questions. So with your permission, do you know -- or, rather, you mention in your report, and I believe that you have been there several times, where is Babin Kuk?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the end of a peninsula which lies to the north-west of the city itself which juts out into the Adriatic. Again, this would be much easier if I could just point to a map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm satisfied with the answer. I seek no more. Do you know where park Gradac is, the park of Gradac?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite close to the city walls, on the side with the -- this would be the north-east side, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where Bogisica park is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, actually. The name is familiar, but I can't immediately put a finger on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Do you know where Lapad is approximately?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, if we start from the Gruz inlet, Lapad is the peninsula that lies to the west of that, so the seaward side of the bay of Gruz or the inlet of Gruz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards all these localities that I refer to, Babin Kuk and Lapad, for instance, is there a large number of hotels there or, rather, was there a large number of hotels there in 1991? Do you know about the hotels in Babin Kuk, Lapad, the hotels of Lapad?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The hotels tend naturally to be built on the coast and as far as Babin Kuk is concerned, there was a -- there was an earlier hotel there, the Neptun, which was built up quite early in the development of Dubrovnik, but the greater development of Babin Kuk as a hotel area took place quite late. I've forgotten the exact date. I know it was as a result of a world bank study. And a group of luxury hotels was built there out at the end of a rather unattractive, if I may say so, by Dalmatian standards a scrubby peninsula sticking out in the sea. This included places like the -- The President was, I suppose, the most expensive of them. The Lapad hotels were gathered around the -- for the most part, if not on the coast very close to the coast, around the -- the bay of Lapad, the little inlet that runs alongside Lapad, the other side of the Gruz inlet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the Libertas Hotel is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That looks directly across to -- to the Old Town. I've forgot what the name of that particular little bay is, but yes, I know where it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to put a question to you, fully aware of the fact that you were not in Dubrovnik in 1991 and I do not expect you to say anything about what happened in October, November, December 1991 and the beginning of 1992. I shall proceed from the following assumption: For example, had the Hotel Libertas been a legitimate military target - I'm not asking you to say whether it was or it wasn't, but let us assume that it was - would you be afraid that this hotel could be damaged as a result of the fact that it was a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it were a legitimate military target it would be damaged, certainly. I mean, I'm puzzled as to the direction of your question. And indeed it was seriously damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. For instance, if the hotels in Lapad were a legitimate military target - I'm not saying they were, and I'm not saying that you could know, but had they been an objective military target, would there have been a great danger of having these hotels damaged to a considerable extent had they been legitimate military targets?
